reference_title: Design and Construction of Mechanically Stabilized Earth Walls and Reinforced Soil Slopes – Volume I
chapter_title: Design of MSE Walls for Extreme Events

sections.title: Introduction to Extreme Event Design
sections.body: Per AASHTO (2007), an extreme event is one whose recurrence interval can be thought to exceed design life. AASHTO (2007) has two limit states for such events: Extreme Event I and Extreme Event II. In the context of MSE walls, the extreme events requiring consideration in design are: seismic events (Extreme Event I), vehicular impact events (Extreme Event II), and superflood events and scour (Extreme Event II).
key_points: Extreme events have recurrence intervals exceeding the structure design life
AASHTO Extreme Event I applies to seismic events
AASHTO Extreme Event II applies to vehicular impact and superflood/scour events
sections.applicability: All MSE walls subject to seismic, vehicular impact, or flood/scour hazards

sections.title: Seismic Events
sections.body: Seismic events are analyzed under the Extreme Event I limit state per AASHTO (2007). Seismic events affect both external and internal stability of MSE walls. The guidance in this section is based on Anderson et al. (2008) and Kavazanjian (2009) and represents updated procedures to those in AASHTO (2007). The design methodology uses a displacement-based approach.
key_points: Seismic design uses Extreme Event I limit state
Guidance based on Anderson et al. (2008) and Kavazanjian (2009) — updated from AASHTO (2007)
Displacement-based approach used for external stability
sections.applicability: MSE walls in seismically active areas

sections.title: Seismic External Stability
sections.body:
External seismic stability uses a displacement-based approach with the following 13-step procedure:

Step 1: Establish initial wall design for static loading using Chapters 4, 5, and 6.

Step 2: Establish seismic hazard using AASHTO (2007) Article 3.10.2. Using 1,000-yr return period seismic hazard maps, estimate: site peak ground acceleration (PGA), and spectral acceleration at 1-second period (S1).

Step 3: Determine Site Effects per AASHTO (2007) Article 3.10.3. Determine Site Class per Article 3.10.3.1 and Site Factors Fpga and Fv from Tables 3.10.3.2-1 and 3.10.3.2-3. Applicable to Site Classes A, B, C, D, and E. For Site Class F, site-specific geotechnical investigations and dynamic site response analysis are required.

Step 4: Determine the maximum acceleration kmax and peak ground velocity (PGV) using Equations 7-1 and 7-2:
  kmax = Fpga × PGA
  PGV = 38 × Fv × S1 (in/s)

Step 5: Using a wall height-dependent reduction factor α, obtain the average peak ground acceleration kav within the reinforced soil zone using Equation 7-3:
  kav = α × kmax
For Site Class C, D, and E (soils), Equation 7-4 gives:
  α = 1.45 – kmax (for kmax ≤ 0.45)
For Site Class A and B (hard and soft rock), α values from Equation 7-4 should be increased by 20 percent. For walls less than approximately 20 ft in height on very firm ground (Site Class B or C), kav ≈ kmax. For wall heights greater than 100 ft, site-specific investigations and dynamic site response analysis are required.

Step 6: Determine the total (static + dynamic) thrust PAE using one of two methods:

Method 1 — Mononobe-Okabe (M-O) formulation (Equation 7-5):
  PAE = 0.5 × γb × h² × KAE
where h is the wall height along the vertical plane within the reinforced soil mass, γb is the unit weight of the retained fill, and KAE is determined from Equation 7-6. The total thrust PAE is assumed to act at h/2 (mid-height of the vertical plane), with stress distributed uniformly over height h. The horizontal seismic coefficient kh = kmax; vertical coefficient kv = 0 (typical assumption).

Limitations of M-O formulation: (1) For backfills sloped at 3H:1V or steeper, solutions may not exist for certain variable combinations; (2) Strictly applicable to homogeneous cohesionless soils — not reliable for c-φ soils, non-uniform backslope profiles, or complex surface loadings. For these cases, use the graphical Culmann method, Coulomb's trial wedge method, or Method 2.

Method 2 — Generalized Limit Equilibrium (GLE) slope stability:
  a. Define wall geometry, nominal surface loadings, groundwater profile, and design soil properties. Model the earth pressure calculation plane as a free boundary — a vertical plane at distance h/2 from back of wall facing (Figure 7-2).
  b. Use Spencer's method (satisfies force and moment equilibrium).
  c. Use circular, linear, bi-linear, or block sliding surface search.
  d. Use kh = kav and kv = 0.
  e. Apply earth pressure PAE on the vertical plane. Examine application points between h/3 and 2h/3 from the base; determine maximum PAE at CDR = 1.0.
  f. Verify design assumptions from output slice loads.
  g. Apply final PAE at mid-height (h/2) for subsequent steps.

Step 7: Determine the horizontal inertial force PIR of the total reinforced wall mass (Equation 7-7):
  PIR = kav × W
where W is the weight of the full reinforced soil mass and any overlying permanent slopes and/or permanent surcharges within the reinforced soil mass limits. PIR acts at the centroid of mass W.

Step 8: Check sliding stability with resistance factor φ = 1.0 and full nominal weight of reinforced zone. Compute total horizontal force THF:
  For M-O method: THF = horizontal component of PAE × cos δ + PIR + γEQ × qLS × KAE × H + other horizontal nominal forces (load factor = 1.0)
  For GLE method: THF = horizontal component of PAE + PIR
Compute sliding resistance R = ΣV × tan δ where δ = minimum of tan φ'r, tan φ'f, or tan δ for continuous reinforcement (see Section 4.5.6.a), and ΣV = W + PAE sin δ + permanent nominal surcharge loads.
  CDRsliding = R / THF
If CDRsliding > 1.0, design is satisfactory — go to Step 11. If not, go to Step 9.

Step 9: Determine the wall yield seismic coefficient ky (coefficient at which wall sliding is initiated) by iterative analysis:
  a. Determine PAE as a function of seismic coefficient k (< kmax) — Figure 7-3a.
  b. Plot horizontal driving and resisting forces vs. k — Figure 7-3b. ky corresponds to the point where CDR against sliding equals 1.0.

Step 10: Determine wall sliding displacement d (in inches) using Equations 7-8 and 7-9, based on ky/kmax, kmax, and PGV, with separate formulas for Western United States (WUS) and Central and Eastern United States (CEUS) per Figure 7-4.

Step 11: Evaluate limiting eccentricity and bearing resistance using Chapter 4 principles with all applicable Extreme Event I loads. Limit state criteria:
  1. Limiting eccentricity: resultant within middle 2/3 of wall base for γEQ = 0.0; within middle 8/10 of wall base for γEQ = 1.0; interpolate linearly.
  2. Bearing resistance: compare effective uniform bearing pressure to nominal bearing resistance based on full reinforced zone width. Resistance factor = 1.0 per AASHTO (2007) Article 10.5.5.3.3.

Step 12: If Step 11 criteria not met, adjust wall geometry and repeat Steps 6 to 11.

Step 13: If Step 11 criteria are met, assess acceptability of sliding displacement d. Typical practice limits lateral displacement to 2.0 in. (50 mm) to 4.0 in. (100 mm), assuming structures at the top or toe of the wall can tolerate such displacements.
key_points: 13-step displacement-based procedure for seismic external stability
kmax = Fpga × PGA; kav = α × kmax where α = 1.45 – kmax for soils (Site Class C/D/E); rock sites increase α by 20%
Two methods for PAE: Mononobe-Okabe (simple) and GLE slope stability (complex geometries or c-φ soils)
PIR = kav × W — inertial force of reinforced soil mass
Sliding CDR ≥ 1.0 with φ = 1.0; if not met, determine yield coefficient ky and estimate displacement d
Limiting eccentricity: middle 2/3 for γEQ = 0; middle 8/10 for γEQ = 1.0
Bearing resistance factor = 1.0 for Extreme Event I
Acceptable sliding displacement typically limited to 50–100 mm (2–4 in.)

sections.title: Seismic Internal Stability
sections.body:
For internal stability, the active wedge is assumed to develop an internal dynamic force Pi equal to the product of the mass in the active zone and the wall height-dependent average seismic coefficient kav (Equation 7-10):
  Pi = kav × Wa
where Wa is the soil weight of the active zone (shaded area in Figure 7-5) and kav is from Equation 7-3. Pi acts at the centroid of the active zone. If the weight of the facing is significant, include it in Wa.

The supplementary inertial force Pi leads to dynamic increases in maximum tensile forces. Reinforcements must resist horizontal forces from Pi in addition to static forces. During seismic internal stability evaluation, the location and maximum tensile force lines are assumed not to change under seismic loading.

The inertial force Pi is distributed equally to all n reinforcement layers (Equation 7-11):
  Tmd = Pi / n
where Tmd is the factored incremental dynamic inertia force at layer i.

The load factor for seismic forces is 1.0. Total factored load per unit wall width is (Equation 7-12):
  Ttotal = Tmax + Tmd
where Tmax is the factored static load from Chapters 4 and 6.
key_points: Internal dynamic force Pi = kav × Wa; distributed equally among all n reinforcement layers as Tmd = Pi/n
Total factored seismic load: Ttotal = Tmax + Tmd
Load factor for seismic forces = 1.0
Location and maximum tensile force lines are assumed unchanged during seismic loading

sections.title: Tensile Failure — Seismic
sections.body:
Metallic reinforcement corrosion loss adjustments for seismic are identical to static analysis. Seismic resistance factors for metallic reinforcements (AASHTO Table 11.5.6-1) for combined static + earthquake loading:
  Strip reinforcements: φ = 1.00
  Grid reinforcements: φ = 0.85

For geosynthetic reinforcements, no creep reduction is applied for the short-duration dynamic component since creep requires long-term sustained loading. The static component Tmax must include creep reduction, but the dynamic component Tmd does not. Geosynthetic reinforcement is designed as follows:

For the static component (Equation 7-13):
  Srs = (Tmax × RF) / (φ × Rc)
where RF = RFCR × RFID × RFD, φ = 1.20 (AASHTO Table 11.5.6-1), Rc = reinforcement coverage ratio.

For the dynamic component (Equation 7-14):
  Srt = (Tmd × RFID × RFD) / (φ × Rc)
(creep reduction factor RFCR excluded from dynamic component)

Required ultimate tensile resistance (Equation 7-15):
  Tult ≥ Srs + Srt
key_points: Metallic seismic resistance factors: strip φ = 1.00, grid φ = 0.85
Geosynthetic seismic: no creep reduction (RFCR) for dynamic component Tmd — creep requires sustained loading
Static component Srs includes full RF = RFCR × RFID × RFD; dynamic Srt excludes RFCR
Resistance factor φ = 1.20 for combined static/earthquake geosynthetic loading
Required Tult ≥ Srs + Srt

sections.title: Pullout Failure — Seismic
sections.body:
For pullout of steel or geosynthetic reinforcement under seismic loading (Equation 7-16):
  Pr = φ × F* × α × σv × C × Le × Rc ≥ Ttotal
where Le is the reinforcement length in the resisting zone, Ttotal is the maximum factored tension from Equation 7-12, φ = 1.20 (AASHTO Table 11.5.6-1), and other terms are as defined in Chapter 4.

For seismic loading conditions, the value of F* (pullout resistance factor) is reduced to 80 percent of the value used for static design, unless dynamic pullout tests are performed to directly determine the F* value.
key_points: Seismic pullout resistance factor φ = 1.20 (AASHTO Table 11.5.6-1)
F* reduced to 80% of static value under seismic loading unless dynamic pullout tests determine F* directly
Design pullout against Ttotal = Tmax + Tmd

sections.title: Seismic Facing Reinforcement Connections
sections.body:
Facing elements are designed to resist the total factored load Ttotal = Tmax + Tmd. Facing elements are designed per applicable provisions of AASHTO (2007) Sections 5, 6, and 8 for reinforced concrete, steel, and timber, respectively.

For segmental concrete block (MBW) faced walls, blocks above the uppermost reinforcement layer must be designed to resist toppling failure during seismic loading.

For geosynthetic connections subject to seismic loading, the factored long-term connection strength Tac must exceed Ttotal. For connections partially or fully dependent on friction between facing blocks and reinforcement, connection strength is reduced to 80% of its static value:

For the static component (Equation 7-17):
  Srs = (Tmax × RFD × CRcr) / (φ × Rc) where φ = 1.20

For the dynamic component (Equation 7-18):
  Srt = (0.8 × Tmd × CRu) / (φ × Rc)
(0.8 multiplier reflects 80% reduction for friction-dependent connections; remove 0.8 for mechanical connections)

Required ultimate tensile resistance at connection (Equation 7-19):
  Tult ≥ Srs + Srt

For metallic reinforcement connections, AASHTO (2007) resistance factors for combined static/seismic:
  Strip reinforcements: φ = 1.00
  Grid reinforcements: φ = 0.85

For seismic cases requiring analysis per AASHTO Section 4, MBW unit walls should use shear resisting devices (shear keys, structural pins from steel or HDPE meeting design life requirements) and should not be fully dependent on frictional resistance for connection capacity.
key_points: Facing connections designed for Ttotal = Tmax + Tmd
Friction-dependent geosynthetic connection strength reduced to 80% under seismic loading
MBW units in seismic areas must use shear keys or structural pins — cannot rely on friction alone
Metallic connection resistance factors: strip φ = 1.00, grid φ = 0.85 for seismic
Required connection Tult ≥ Srs + Srt

sections.title: Vehicular Impact Events
sections.body: Traffic railing impact loads are analyzed under Extreme Event II limit state per AASHTO (2007) Article A13.2. Vehicular impact events affect only the internal stability of MSE walls. Guidance is based on NCHRP 22-20 (Bligh et al., 2009), which extends previous FHWA methods (Elias et al., 2001) based on laboratory and full-scale field tests. Guidance for post and beam railings is based on AASHTO (2007).
key_points: Vehicular impact analyzed under Extreme Event II limit state
Impact affects only internal stability (not external stability)
Guidance from NCHRP 22-20 (Bligh et al., 2009)
sections.applicability: MSE walls with traffic barriers or guardrails

sections.title: Traffic Barriers — Vehicular Impact Design
sections.body:
Traffic barriers over the front face of MSE walls must be designed to resist overturning moment by their own mass per AASHTO (2007) Article 11.10.10.2.

Static Impact Load: The recommended static impact force is 10,000 lb (45 kN) applied on a barrier with minimum height of 32 in. (810 mm) above the roadway. Bligh et al. (2009) found that a 10,000 lb (45 kN) static impact load is equivalent to a dynamic TL-4 test level of 54,000 lb (240 kN). Where the impact barrier moment slab is cast integrally with concrete pavement, the additional force may be neglected.

Load Combination and Factors for Extreme Event II: load factor γP-EV = 1.35 for static soil load; traffic surcharge modeled as equivalent 2 ft soil height uses γP-EV = 1.35 (not γ = 0.50) for internal stability; static equivalent impact loads use load factor γCT = 1.00.

Reinforcement Rupture: The static impact force adds additional horizontal forces to the upper 2 reinforcement layers:
  Layer 1 (top): rupture impact load = 2,300 lb/lft (33.5 kN/m)
  Layer 2: rupture impact load = 600 lb/lft (8.8 kN/m)
Distribution of stresses per AASHTO (2007) Figure 3.11.6.3-2 is NOT recommended.

Load factor for impact = 1.0. Total factored reinforcement load (Equations 7-20a and 7-20b):
  Ttotal = Tmax + TI
  TI = ti / Rc
where ti = 33.5 kN/m for layer 1 or 8.8 kN/m for layer 2, and Rc = reinforcement coverage ratio.

Note: for geosynthetic reinforcements, the nominal strength used for impact sizing is NOT increased by eliminating the creep reduction factor (unlike seismic design), because full-scale traffic barrier impact testing with geosynthetic reinforcement has not been performed.

Reinforcement Pullout: Impact pullout resistance is mobilized over the full reinforcement length L (not just the resistant zone). Traffic surcharge (2 ft equivalent height) is included in nominal vertical stress σv for pullout resistance. Impact pullout design loads:
  Layer 1 (top): pullout impact load = 1,300 lb/lft (19.0 kN/m)
  Layer 2: pullout impact load = 600 lb/lft (8.8 kN/m)

Resistance Factors: Use Table 4-7 factors for "Combined static/traffic barrier impact" for Extreme Event II. Pullout resistance factor = 1.00 for both metallic and geosynthetic reinforcements.

Barrier, Coping, and Moment Slab: Typical base slab length = 20 ft (6 m), jointed to adjacent slabs with shear dowels. Parapet reinforcement per AASHTO Section 13 Railings. Anchoring slab must resist the ultimate strength of the standard parapet and provide adequate sliding and overturning resistance.

MSE Facing Panel Design: Upper facing panel must be separated from barrier slab with 1 to 2 in. (25–50 mm) of expanded polystyrene (see Figure 5-2(b)). Separation allows the barrier and slab to resist impact load without stressing the facing panel.
key_points: Static equivalent impact force = 10,000 lb (45 kN) ≡ dynamic TL-4 = 54,000 lb (240 kN)
Impact load factor γCT = 1.00; soil γP-EV = 1.35; surcharge γP-EV = 1.35
Rupture impact: Layer 1 = 33.5 kN/m, Layer 2 = 8.8 kN/m
Pullout impact: Layer 1 = 19.0 kN/m, Layer 2 = 8.8 kN/m
Geosynthetic impact design does NOT remove creep reduction factor (insufficient test data)
Pullout resistance factor = 1.00 for impact loading
Upper panel must be separated from barrier slab by 25–50 mm expanded polystyrene

sections.title: Post and Beam Railings
sections.body: Flexible post and beam barriers shall be placed at a minimum distance of 3.0 ft (0.9 m) from the wall face, driven 5.0 ft (1.5 m) below grade, and spaced to miss the reinforcements where possible. If the reinforcements cannot be avoided, the wall must be designed accounting for the presence of an obstruction. Each of the upper two rows of reinforcement shall be designed for an additional horizontal load of 150 lb/lft (2.2 kN/m) per wall length, for a total additional load of 300 lb/lft (4.4 kN/m).
key_points: Minimum 3.0 ft (0.9 m) clearance from wall face to post and beam barrier
Posts driven 5.0 ft (1.5 m) below grade
Additional 150 lb/lft (2.2 kN/m) per upper two reinforcement rows = 300 lb/lft (4.4 kN/m) total additional load
Design as obstruction per Chapter 5 if reinforcements cannot be avoided
sections.applicability: MSE walls with flexible post and beam railings at the wall crest

sections.title: Superflood Events and Scour
sections.body:
The stability of walls and abutments in areas of turbulent flow must be addressed in design. Wall design is based on total scour depths estimated per AASHTO (2007) Article 2.6.4.4.2. Scour must be investigated for two flood conditions:

Design Flood: The more severe of the 100-year event or an overtopping flood of lesser recurrence interval. Stability design assumes all streambed material above the total scour line has been removed. Analyzed as a strength limit state.

Check Flood: The more severe of the 500-year event or an overtopping flood of lesser recurrence interval. Stability design assumes all streambed material above the total scour line has been removed. This is an extreme event condition — Extreme Event II limit state applies. Resistance factors may be taken as 1.0 per AASHTO (2007) Articles 10.6.4 and 10.5.5.3.3.
key_points: Design flood = 100-year event or overtopping flood; analyzed at strength limit state
Check flood = 500-year event or overtopping flood; analyzed at Extreme Event II limit state
Both floods analyzed assuming all material above total scour line is removed
Check flood resistance factors = 1.0 per AASHTO Articles 10.6.4 and 10.5.5.3.3
sections.applicability: MSE walls and abutments in areas subject to scour from flooding or turbulent flow
